title: Floating-Point Division by Zero Rejected Instead of IEEE 754 Semantics
pattern: A floating-point arithmetic helper returns `Result::Err` or throws on division by zero (or other IEEE-defined edge cases) instead of returning the IEEE 754 result (`INFINITY`, `-INFINITY`, `NaN`).
why_bad: IEEE 754 already defines these results, and `inf`/`NaN` propagate through subsequent operations without handling at every step. Wrapping each division in a `Result` forces error plumbing through numeric pipelines and hides the standard semantics numeric code relies on, such as `is_finite()` checks at the end of a computation.
detection: A function over `f32`/`f64` that checks `b == 0.0` (or `b.abs() < EPS` used as an equality test) and returns `Err`/throws before performing `a / b`.
counterexample: Integer division, where no IEEE sentinel exists; domain boundaries where a non-finite value must not escape (currency, serialization to formats without `NaN`, control outputs to actuators), which should validate and reject there; and code that needs to tell the caller which input caused the non-finite value.
source: Martin Fowler, *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture*, p. 350; Andrew Hunt & David Thomas, *The Pragmatic Programmer*, p. 308.
